claim: According to ESOHR (European Saudi Organisation for Human Rights, Berlin), 59 of the 108 people executed in Saudi Arabia from January to June 2026 (about 54%) were foreigners, including 49 of the 71 executed for drug offences, and Bangladeshis were among the 108, though how many is not known.
target_section: NEW: Arrested abroad: trials, drug charges and the death penalty
why_new: Execution numbers including Bangladeshis; nothing in the guide.

claim: According to Amnesty International, 597 people were executed in Saudi Arabia for drug offences alone from January 2014 to June 2025, about 75% of them foreigners, in a country where about 44% of the 3 crore 53 lakh population is foreign.
target_section: NEW: Arrested abroad: trials, drug charges and the death penalty
why_new: Long-run drug-execution figure.

claim: Two Bangladeshis convicted of an 'immoral act' in a mosque in Mecca were executed in Saudi Arabia shortly before October 2026, outside the January to June 2026 count.
target_section: NEW: Arrested abroad: trials, drug charges and the death penalty
why_new: A dated Bangladeshi case.

claim: Bangladeshis are the largest group of foreign workers in Saudi Arabia, at least 25 lakh, followed by Indians, Pakistanis, Yemenis and Egyptians, yet ESOHR said it could learn or record nothing about 91 of the 108 cases (84.2%) executed in early 2026 before the execution, so there is no answer on how many Bangladeshis are held, on what charges, or whether they had lawyers, interpreters or consular help.
target_section: NEW: Arrested abroad: trials, drug charges and the death penalty
why_new: Size of exposure and the information gap (a Need to know).

claim: According to Prothom Alo, Saudi Arabia's 2013 Law of Criminal Procedure gives accused people the right to legal help at both the investigation and trial stages and bans torture, but ESOHR documented that death-row prisoners in Khamis Mushait, Najran and Tabuk prisons had no professional interpreter or legal help, did not understand the proceedings, and often did not know when their sentence was upheld or their plea for pardon rejected.
target_section: NEW: Arrested abroad: trials, drug charges and the death penalty
why_new: The right on paper against practice.

claim: Amnesty International documented 25 foreign nationals convicted of drug offences in Saudi Arabia (from Egypt, Ethiopia, Jordan, Pakistan and Somalia) and found many went through the system alone, without understanding or receiving the court papers or charges, without consular help, and at risk of confessions taken without an adequate interpreter or lawyer.
target_section: NEW: Arrested abroad: trials, drug charges and the death penalty
why_new: What an arrested migrant faces in court.

claim: Amnesty International says Saudi law has no clear rule on advance notice of an execution to the prisoner or family; families said the prisoner may at most phone 24 hours before, some were told by prison officers the day before 'your turn has come', and many families learned of an execution from other prisoners' calls or from the state news agency.
target_section: NEW: Arrested abroad: trials, drug charges and the death penalty
why_new: What families should expect; nothing in the guide.

claim: Saudi law does not guarantee return of the body after an execution, and in all three of the 25 Amnesty-documented cases executed between January and June 2025, Saudi Arabia neither returned the body to the family nor told them where it was buried.
target_section: NEW: Arrested abroad: trials, drug charges and the death penalty
why_new: Body repatriation does not happen after execution; relevant to 'How is the body brought home?'.

claim: Amnesty's review found that low education, poor language skills and lack of money harm these migrants twice: first in migration, when they are cheated or exploited by brokers from the very start of going to Saudi Arabia, and then if they face legal trouble there, when they cannot hire a good lawyer or defend themselves properly and in most cases have reduced access to consular help.
target_section: NEW: Arrested abroad: trials, drug charges and the death penalty
why_new: Links dalal exploitation to later legal vulnerability.

claim: In December 2024 the UN Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination found racial and ethnic discrimination in Saudi Arabia's criminal justice system, with migrant workers and domestic workers, including women, subjected to arbitrary detention, torture and ill-treatment, and called on Saudi Arabia to impose a moratorium on the death penalty.
target_section: NEW: Arrested abroad: trials, drug charges and the death penalty
why_new: UN finding; likely fluff for the guide unless the new section is kept.

claim: Prothom Alo's October 2026 article lists among its sources Amnesty International's report 'If We Had Money and a Lawyer, Maybe My Brother Would Be Alive': Saudi Arabia's Execution Crisis (7 July 2025), ESOHR's '108 Saudi Arabia: Executions in the First Half of 2026', and a joint MENA Rights Group, ALQST and ESOHR submission dated 10 March 2026 to the UN Special Rapporteur on extrajudicial, summary or arbitrary executions.
target_section: NEW: Arrested abroad: trials, drug charges and the death penalty
why_new: Pointer to primary sources.

claim: Abdullah Al Zobayer, who returned from captivity in Libya in 2024, said the ring that took him has many members and also targets Bangladeshi expatriates in the Middle East, taking people to Libya with talk of good jobs or passage to Europe and holding them hostage to collect money from their families.
target_section: Recruited while abroad or just back
why_new: A survivor stating that the ring recruits among expatriates already in the Middle East.

claim: Afaz Uddin Molla, a worker in Kuwait, told Prothom Alo that in August 2024 he answered a Facebook advert offering a cheap route to Canada and was promised he would be taken from Kuwait to Canada, and according to the case statement the man calling himself Asadul took BDT 24 lakh from him by December 2024.
target_section: Recruited while abroad or just back
why_new: Another worker targeted while in the Gulf, this time online.

claim: Ali Hossain of Mymensingh told Prothom Alo in November 2025 that his son Afzal Hossain Meraj, who went to Russia on 10 August 2024 through the travel agency Friendship and Co-operative Recruitment, worked four months at the company he was recruited for, was then laid off, and then went to fight through a ring; he was wounded in a mine blast and spent 25 days in hospital.
target_section: Recruited while abroad or just back
placement: other: In Russia, after the job ends
why_new: Another dated, named case of the lay-off-then-army pattern, with the agency named and the four-month gap.

claim: One of the 113 returnees told the ambassador he had lived in Libya for 14 years before deciding, in old age, to try the 'game' (the boat crossing to Italy).
target_section: Recruited while abroad or just back
why_new: Long-settled workers in Libya also take the boat; the section has Gulf and Russia examples only.

claim: The victim in the June 2026 Australia online case was a Bangladeshi working in Oman, approached in December 2025 through a person he already knew.
target_section: Recruited while abroad or just back
why_new: Another Gulf-based worker targeted for an onward move.

claim: Mannan Soyal, a Bangladeshi who returned from a scam centre in Cambodia, told a roundtable on technology-driven fraud and human trafficking held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 22 July 2026 that he went to Saudi Arabia in 2022, stayed there three years and decided to go abroad again after coming home, and that a relative from his area then sent him to Cambodia for BDT 5 lakh with talk of a restaurant job.
target_section: Recruited while abroad or just back
placement: other: new bullet (a Gulf returnee recruited for Cambodia)
why_new: The section has returnees recruited for Libya and Russia but none recruited for Cambodia after a Gulf stint.

claim: Shariful Islam Hasan, associate director of BRAC's Migration Programme and Youth Platform, told a roundtable on technology-driven fraud and human trafficking held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 22 July 2026 that many people who are in Malaysia are being cheated with assurances that they will be sent to Australia.
target_section: Recruited while abroad or just back
why_new: The section covers recruitment in the Gulf, on the flight home and in Russia; this adds Malaysia with an Australia promise.

claim: The UN commission says foreigners already in Russia were also taken into the armed forces by deception or coercion: some were in police custody or in temporary detention centres for foreign nationals and some were serving prison sentences, and several were told that signing a military contract would spare them prosecution, a long sentence, solitary confinement or torture, with threats of torture or a longer sentence if they did not sign.
target_section: Recruited while abroad or just back
placement: other: In Russia, after the job ends
why_new: A recruitment point the guide lacks: foreigners in Russian police custody, immigration detention or prison.

claim: According to the family of Jafar Sardar of Jashore, reported on 17 February 2025, the broker took 10 Bangladeshis to Russia together; one, a young man from Narsingdi named Akram, escaped and came home, and the other nine were forced to the battlefield in Ukraine to fight for Russia, where one was killed and one was shot.
why_new: The outcome for the whole group of 10 sent in 2024 (one escaped, nine sent to the front, one dead, one shot); the guide's Russia section covers only the May 2026 group in detail.

claim: Jafar Sardar's wife, Khadija Akter, told Prothom Alo in February 2025 that the broker ring forcibly took her husband to the Russian battlefield, that he was kept in a barracks, given an army haircut and war training, and that his last message said 'bring me home at any cost'.
why_new: A family account of what happens between arrival and deployment.

claim: Relatives of nine Bangladeshis sent to the Ukraine battlefield formed human chains in Dhaka several times, went more than once to the Russian embassy and to Bangladesh's Foreign Ministry and wrote to the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry, and on 16 February 2025 Jafar Sardar's family wrote to the Chief Adviser's office asking for his return and the money; the report of 17 February 2025 records no result.
why_new: Shows which doors families actually tried in early 2025 and that the article reports no outcome.

claim: A report by BRAC's Migration Programme, 'Promises Written in Blood: How Legal Migration Turned into Forced Recruitment in the Russia-Ukraine War', published on the Monday before 5 November 2025 and based on survivors' accounts, family testimony and document checks, says brokers lured workers with false promises of high-paid work, that many went hoping for work in oil, construction or logistics, and that after arrival in Russia their passports were confiscated and they were forced to join the military.
why_new: Adds the BRAC report by name, its evidence base, and the oil and logistics job pitches (the guide has construction and welding).

claim: BRAC's November 2025 report says the Bangladeshis spent BDT 7 to 8 lakh to go to Russia for work, and that international facilitators as well as local brokers are involved in trapping them.
why_new: A 2025 price point (BDT 7 to 8 lakh) below the BDT 9.5 to 10 lakh the guide gives for 2026, and BRAC's finding of international facilitators.

claim: Shariful Hasan, BRAC's associate director (migration and youth), told Prothom Alo in November 2025 that 10 families had so far asked BRAC to bring relatives back from Russia and that these men had gone to Russia on valid visas to work; BRAC's report says there are more such Bangladeshis but the number could not be confirmed.
why_new: BRAC's own caseload as of November 2025 and its statement that the true number is unknown.

claim: According to Prothom Alo in November 2025, BRAC's Migration Programme began receiving many applications from families from late 2024 with almost the same account, submitted applications to the Foreign Ministry for the victims' rescue, gave case documents to the police's Criminal Investigation Department (CID), and gives the families legal and psychological support.
why_new: Says concretely what BRAC does with a family's application (Foreign Ministry rescue application, case papers to CID, legal and psychosocial support); the guide only says BRAC asked the government to trace the men.

claim: Shariful Hasan of BRAC said in November 2025 that a Bangladeshi using the name MD Sohel was campaigning on Facebook about the benefits available for joining the Russian army and fighting, and that because of this many people were being newly lured to go to Russia to fight.
why_new: A recruitment channel the section lacks: open Facebook promotion of army service by a Bangladeshi.

claim: BRAC's November 2025 report records that Ayon Mondal of Bagerhat, who went to Russia on a valid visa, said in his last message that he was being taken towards the Ukrainian border and has not been traced since, and that Amit Barua of Cumilla has been missing since a photo showed him in Russian military uniform.
why_new: Two named missing men from 2025 who went on valid visas.

claim: Ali Hossain applied to the Foreign Ministry on 22 April 2025 to bring his son Afzal Hossain Meraj home, alleging in the letter that his son had been sold to the Russian army, and told Prothom Alo in November 2025 that his son had been able to return two months earlier with the help of the Bangladesh Embassy in Moscow.
why_new: A second documented return through the Moscow embassy, with the route the family used (a written application to the Foreign Ministry) and the time it took (about five months).

claim: Tasneem Siddiqui, executive director of RMMRU (the Refugee and Migratory Movements Research Unit), told Prothom Alo in November 2025 that besides people going to Russia directly for work, many are first taken to Saudi Arabia on tourist or Umrah visas and are later made to sign a contract and forced to go to the battlefield.
why_new: Names Saudi Arabia on a tourist or Umrah visa as a first leg; the guide's path lists Dubai and unnamed third countries.

claim: An AFP report of 12 April 2025, as cited by Prothom Alo, quoted the Bangladesh Embassy in Moscow as saying about a dozen families had contacted it to get their sons back, all alleging the sons were deceived into the Russian army, and reported that Mohammad Yasin Sheikh, 22, was killed on 27 March 2025 while fighting for Russian forces.
why_new: The embassy's own caseload in April 2025 and a named, dated death earlier than any in the guide.

claim: Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mohammad Rafiqul Alam said at a Dhaka briefing on 9 February 2025 that some Bangladeshis had been forced into the Russia-Ukraine war after falling into the hands of human traffickers, that the Ministry had asked the Embassy in Moscow for details, that the relevant ministries had been asked to act against the recruiting and travel agencies involved, and that one member of a ring trafficking people to Russia had been arrested.
why_new: The government's first public acknowledgement and first arrest, in February 2025; the guide's law entries start in June 2026.

claim: According to the Foreign Ministry spokesperson's 9 February 2025 briefing, the authorities concerned were asked to take special caution at Bangladesh's international airports over Bangladeshis going to Russia on travel visas during the war and those with a valid Russian travel visa in their passports.
why_new: An airport-side measure: a passenger for Russia on a travel visa can expect extra scrutiny at departure since February 2025.

claim: Prothom Alo reported in November 2025 that RMMRU (the Refugee and Migratory Movements Research Unit) had prepared a report from interviews with victims about a month and a half earlier and given it to the adviser for the Information Ministry with a call to raise awareness.
why_new: Existence of a second victim-interview report (RMMRU, about September 2025) besides BRAC's.

claim: A Prothom Alo editorial of 4 February 2026, citing an Associated Press (AP) investigation, says people from disadvantaged areas were taken to Russia with the lure of work as cooks or cleaners and, after arriving, were forced to sign military contracts written in Russian.
why_new: Adds cook and cleaner as job pitches, from the AP investigation.

claim: According to the AP investigation as summarised in a Prothom Alo editorial of 4 February 2026, a Russian commander told one victim directly that he had in fact been 'sold'; returned workers said they were made to collect bodies from the battlefield and move the wounded, and those who refused were tortured.
why_new: Tasks the men were put to (body collection, evacuating the wounded) and the 'sold' statement.

claim: A Prothom Alo editorial of 4 February 2026 said it was believed that at least 40 Bangladeshis had lost their lives in the previous few months after being deceived by recruiting agencies into the Russia-Ukraine war.
why_new: A February 2026 death estimate, earlier than the guide's figures (34 by March 2026 from Fortify Rights, 20 of the May group).

claim: A Prothom Alo editorial of 4 February 2026 said, citing the investigation, that a Bangladeshi living in Moscow is the main organiser of the trafficking ring, that investigators suspect the ring has links with the Russian government, and named 'SP Global' as one of the firms that ran such trafficking openly.
why_new: Who is said to run the chain (a Moscow-based Bangladeshi) and one firm named.

claim: Jahangir Alam of Lakshmipur, who was sent to Russia in 2025 on the promise of work as a cook in a cantonment and was instead sent straight to the battlefield, told Prothom Alo in July 2026 that he was handed a weapon without training and then taught to use it for one day, that 16 men were together in the war camp, and that he lived in fear after four of them died.
why_new: A named survivor with the job pitch 'cook in a cantonment', one day of weapons training and 4 deaths among 16.

claim: Jahangir Alam of Lakshmipur escaped from the battlefield and came home through the Bangladesh embassy seven months after going, according to Prothom Alo in July 2026.
why_new: Another return through the embassy after an escape; the guide has one (August 2026).

claim: RMMRU says 4,727 Bangladeshis went to Russia in 2025 against 993 the year before, and that 2,125 workers took clearance for Russia in the first six months of 2026, Prothom Alo reported on 30 July 2026.
why_new: Year-by-year figures; the guide gives only one combined total (7,449 from January 2025 to 27 October 2026). Note the 2024 figure here (993) differs from the BMET figure in the 21 October 2026 article (1,395).

claim: Expatriates' Welfare Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury told Prothom Alo in July 2026 that the licences of three agencies that sent workers to Russia had been cancelled, that the licences of 49 agencies linked to irregularities in sending workers to Malaysia had been withdrawn, and that BMET had been told to be more careful before giving clearance for Cambodia.
why_new: The Minister's own statement of the three actions together; the 49 Malaysia licences are not in the scam chapter.

claim: Jahangir Alam of Lakshmipur told Prothom Alo in September 2026 that after four men in his war camp died he fell ill and spent two months in hospital, escaped from there, and returned home through the Bangladesh embassy.
why_new: How this survivor got out: escape from hospital, then the embassy.

claim: According to BMET, 4,727 Bangladeshis went to the Russian Federation in 2025, which put Russia 13th among Bangladesh's overseas labour markets that year, ahead of Malaysia, South Korea and Lebanon.
why_new: Russia's rank among destinations in 2025.

claim: Of the 30 Bangladeshis who flew from Dhaka to Russia on 7 May 2026, Prothom Alo reported that after 21 days of training they were split into groups of 16, 8 and 6 and sent to the war, and that many died around 12 and 13 June; two who were hospitalised, Adnan Hossain of Narayanganj and Rajon Hossain of Jhenaidah, later escaped and came home and gave the paper the information about the others' deaths.
why_new: The timeline of the May 2026 group (21 days' training, three groups, deaths around 12-13 June) and the two named survivors who are the source.

claim: Prothom Alo reported that Rajon Hossain (21) of Jhenaidah, who went to Russia with the group of 30 on 7 May 2026, paid a broker BDT 10 lakh for a high-paid job, got no job, and after four days in a hotel was sent to an army camp after his signature was taken on a paper; he told the paper that after 21 days' training he was sent to the front line with five other Bangladeshis, that four were killed in a drone attack, and that he was wounded, admitted to hospital and escaped from there to come home.
why_new: The survivor's own sequence and the fate of his six-man group (four dead); the guide has his account of the contract but not what followed.

claim: Prothom Alo reported that Adnan Hossain of Narayanganj was admitted to a Moscow hospital with a splinter in his abdomen from the battlefield, had three operations, could not get out of bed for a month and a half, and after two months in hospital escaped and went to the embassy, then came home on 15 September 2026 on a travel pass (a valid travel permit).
why_new: The practical way out that worked: reach the embassy in person from hospital and leave on a travel pass.

claim: Adnan Hossain said Russia does not publish information on Bangladeshis' deaths in the war and does not bring back the bodies, and that anyone who does not return from the front line is declared missing; Prothom Alo reported that those it spoke to said the bodies of foreigners killed are not recovered but left on the field.
why_new: Explains why families get neither a body nor a death record: the dead are recorded as missing.

claim: Abdul Majid of Lalmonirhat told Prothom Alo that his son Abdullah Al Mamun phoned his younger brother the day before being sent to fight after training, that there was no contact afterwards, and that a man who went with him, Al Amin, later said Mamun had died; a funeral in absentia was arranged in the village, but because the death was not confirmed the people who came prayed instead of performing the funeral prayer, and five months had passed by October 2026.
why_new: How a family learns of a death (from a fellow recruit) and is left without confirmation.

claim: Prothom Alo reported on 21 October 2026 that it had received news of at least 54 deaths of Bangladeshis in the Russia-Ukraine war over the previous three years.
why_new: The newspaper's own running count (54 in three years), higher than the 34 the guide cites from Fortify Rights.

claim: According to the embassy's 25 May 2026 letter, on 18 May a worker's family phoned the Bangladesh Embassy in Russia to say that 30 people had come through Jabale Noor and RS International and were being sent to the battlefield, and the embassy was sending a letter to Russia's Foreign Ministry asking that the workers be returned to work under their appointment letters instead of being sent to war.
why_new: A family's phone call on 18 May is what alerted the embassy, 11 days after arrival and before deployment; the embassy's response was a letter to the Russian Foreign Ministry.

claim: Foreign Ministry sources told Prothom Alo in October 2026 that for four to five months the Russian government had been informing the embassy about Bangladeshis missing and killed on the battlefield, 40 people so far, without separating the dead from the missing, and had not yet said anything about the latest 20 deaths.
why_new: The only official Russian-side figure: 40 dead or missing notified to the embassy.

claim: Foreign Ministry sources told Prothom Alo in October 2026 that compensation can be claimed if someone dies in the war or is missing for more than six months, but that getting it from Russia means a complicated process that includes establishing who the heir is and the heir going to Russia and staying at least six months, and that the bodies cannot be recovered.
why_new: The compensation rule and why families cannot use it; the guide has nothing on compensation from Russia.

claim: Bangladesh's ambassador to Russia, Md Nazrul Islam, told Prothom Alo in October 2026 that more than 90% of the workers go to the war of their own accord, that Russia has said the latest 30 also went voluntarily and holds written proof of it, and that the bodies cannot be sent home because the Russian authorities are not handing them over.
why_new: The embassy's and Russia's position: the signed contract is treated as written proof of volunteering.

claim: Two wounded returnees and six families told Prothom Alo that the workers pleaded with their families before being sent to war in June 2026, that when the families contacted the agency it promised to take responsibility, and that from the first week of June the men began to go missing; the families got news of deaths but no proof.
why_new: What the agency told families when they called before deployment: a promise to take responsibility, and nothing after.

claim: The Wage Earners' Welfare Board says it bears the cost of bringing home the body of a worker who went with BMET clearance or took membership registration from the embassy after going abroad, on the family's application, and that a family with neither can still apply, in which case the Board sends a proposal to the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry, which pays from a yearly budget allocation.
placement: other: bodies and compensation in Bangladesh
why_new: The body-repatriation rule stated for this context, including the route for a worker with no clearance or membership.

claim: According to the Wage Earners' Welfare Board, it gives BDT 35,000 cash for the burial of each body brought home and then a BDT 3 lakh grant, but by October 2026 no application to bring a body home from Russia had reached it, because with no proof of death nobody can apply, and so nobody is getting any compensation.
placement: other: bodies and compensation in Bangladesh
why_new: Why families of the Russia dead get none of the Welfare Board's death benefits: every benefit starts from proof of death.

claim: The Special Response Battalion (SRB) said that Mizanur Rahman, founder of Jabale Noor International and described as one of the leaders of the trafficking ring, and Abu Taher alias Lentu were arrested on 13 October 2026 over the sending of the 30 men.
why_new: Names, role and date of the two arrests the guide mentions without detail.

claim: CID sources said at least six cases had been filed over the trafficking of Bangladeshis to Russia, Prothom Alo reported on 21 October 2026.
why_new: Number of criminal cases on the Russia route.

claim: BMET data show 37 people took clearance for Russia in 2023, 1,395 in 2024, 4,725 in 2025 and 3,105 in 2026 up to 15 October.
why_new: The year-by-year BMET series; the guide has a single combined figure.

claim: Md Palash Sheikh, one of the 30, was wounded in his first spell at the war, was sent back after recovering and lost a hand, and in October 2026 was being treated in a Moscow hospital; his cousin Abu Saleh Islam told Prothom Alo that asking the embassy and the Ministry had brought no help to get him home, that he cannot escape the hospital because it is under army guard, and that the family, which spent BDT 10 lakh to send him, has received no money.
why_new: A wounded man is sent back to the front; a case where the embassy and Ministry did not help, and the hospital is guarded.

claim: Prothom Alo obtained 28 separate letters that families submitted to the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry in July 2026 to get missing relatives back; the letters say Jabale Noor International of Khilkhet and RS International of Ashulia sent the men to Russia through brokers, that they were sold to the Russian army with the lure of high pay, and ask for their quick and safe return and for financial help.
why_new: 28 written applications to the Ministry in July 2026, with the two agencies' locations as the families give them (Khilkhet and Ashulia); the article reports no result.

claim: Prothom Alo reported in October 2026 that travel to Russia has not decreased, and that because staying six months at the war brings a chance of Russian citizenship and pay of BDT 3 to 4 lakh a month, many go to the war of their own accord.
why_new: The open pitch for army service itself: citizenship after six months and BDT 3 to 4 lakh a month.

claim: A Prothom Alo investigation found that clearances to send workers to Russia were taken in the names of 93 recruiting agencies over four years, that only 17 agencies took clearance for more than a hundred workers each, and that Bonna Bijoy Overseas alone took the most, 27% of the workers or about 2,500.
why_new: How concentrated the Russia business is: one agency with over a quarter of all clearances.

claim: Prothom Alo reported on 21 October 2026 that Bonna Bijoy Overseas, the agency that sent the most workers to Russia, is accused of trafficking in the name of sending workers to Algeria, has a human trafficking case against it and faces allegations over sending workers to Russia too, and that its server has been locked so it can take no new clearances; its managing director, Barun Debnath, did not answer the paper's call or text message.
why_new: Action against the largest Russia sender: its BMET server access locked.

claim: Expatriates' Welfare Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury told Prothom Alo in October 2026 that nobody is being given clearance without verification and attestation of confirmed job information, that many people are going by various means through different countries, and that all embassies have been alerted and instructed to keep watch by staying in touch with the expatriate community.
why_new: The Minister's stated rule (no clearance without attestation) and his admission that people still go through third countries.

claim: Shariful Hasan, head of BRAC's Migration Programme, said in October 2026 that the agencies accused of trafficking are sending the most workers to Russia and that nobody has a count of how many found work, where the rest are or how many have died; he advised opening a hotline and drawing up a list of the missing.
why_new: As of October 2026 there is no hotline and no list of the missing; BRAC proposes both.

claim: The SRB, the detective branch and others concerned told Prothom Alo that the men sent from Bangladesh have neither the physical fitness, the training nor the tactics for war, and that when the enemy attacks them with drones Russian soldiers identify the enemy's position.
why_new: How the 'bait' use works in practice (drawing drone fire so positions can be located); the guide states the fact without the mechanism.

claim: Prothom Alo reported on 21 October 2026 that of the 30 Bangladeshis sent to Russia on 7 May 2026, 20 were reported dead, two were wounded and under treatment in Russian hospitals (Palash Sheikh and Ali Hasan Sohel), two had managed to return to Bangladesh (Rajon Hossain and Adnan Hossain), and six were still being made to fight.
why_new: The full accounting of the 30 (20 dead, 2 in hospital, 2 home, 6 still at the front); the guide gives only the deaths.

claim: According to the SRB's 14 October 2026 press conference, 17 of the 30 died in a drone attack on their first day on the battlefield and three more died later at different times.
why_new: States the cause (a drone attack) and how the 20 divides into 17 and 3.

claim: Pabitra Chandra (30), a carpenter from a very poor family in Gopalpur, Tangail, and one of the 30, went to Russia with BDT 1 lakh 30 thousand from selling his wife's jewellery and BDT 9.5 lakh borrowed from an NGO and local moneylenders, according to Prothom Alo.
why_new: How one of the 30 raised the money: BDT 10.8 lakh, almost all of it debt.

claim: Pabitra Chandra's brother-in-law, Tapan Chandra Sutradhar, told Prothom Alo that in the first few days after reaching Russia Pabitra said he and several others were being kept in a hotel and would be given work once the papers were sorted out, that contact then stopped for some time, and that on 29 May 2026 he phoned to say 'we are being taken to the war by force; the chance of dying there is 95 per cent'.
why_new: What the men were told while held in the hotel ('work after the papers are done') and the date families learned the truth.

claim: Prothom Alo reported that after 29 May 2026 Pabitra Chandra contacted the Bangladesh embassy and asked it to arrange for him and the others to be brought home, that his family later heard of his death through his companions, and that as of 21 October 2026 the family had not had it confirmed by the embassy or any government channel.
why_new: A direct request to the embassy before deployment that did not stop it, and no official confirmation of death five months on.

claim: Tapan Chandra Sutradhar said in October 2026 that lenders come and stand behind Pabitra Chandra's family for their money when they sit down to eat, and that the family is thinking of selling its remaining 3 decimals of land, which would still not clear the debt.
why_new: What the debt does to the family after the death.

claim: Rahat Chowdhury, nephew of Robin Mir, a Siddhirganj (Narayanganj) autorickshaw driver who was one of the 30, told Prothom Alo that for the first three or four days in Russia his uncle was given good food and shown around, that there was then no news for five or six days, that on 15 May 2026 he said they were being taken to work, that on 17 May he was seen in an army camp in a video, and that on 29 May he phoned in tears to say they had been taken through deep forest on the promise of work and sold.
why_new: A day-by-day timeline from arrival to the army camp (good treatment, silence, 'going to work', camp within 10 days).

claim: Robin Mir of Siddhirganj went to Russia for work after selling his village land and cattle and borrowing, with three other men from Narayanganj, through whom his family learned of his death, according to Prothom Alo.
why_new: Another of the 30, financed by selling land and cattle; four men recruited from one district.

claim: Taslim Sardar, who keeps in regular contact with his brother-in-law Sourav Molla of Gopalganj through the messaging app imo, told Prothom Alo in October 2026 that Sourav was three to four kilometres behind the front line being made to dig earth for bunkers, and had twice tried to escape without success.
why_new: What the six survivors still in the army are doing, and that escape attempts fail.

claim: According to Taslim Sardar, of the six men from the group of 30 still at the war in October 2026, Kamal was digging bunkers with Sourav, Roni Sheikh and Al Amin were carrying food, water and weapons on foot from the camp to the front line, and Hanif and Helal had no fixed task and were made sometimes to dig bunkers and sometimes to carry food.
why_new: The support tasks the men are used for.

claim: Taslim Sardar, a relative of one of the six men still at the war, organised a human chain in Dhaka with the affected families shortly before 21 October 2026, Prothom Alo reported.
why_new: Families of the May 2026 group are organised and reachable through a named relative.

claim: According to information from the families, besides Pabitra Chandra and Robin Mir the 18 others of the group of 30 killed on the battlefield are Sohel, Md Mehedi Hasan, Md Al Mamun, Md Abdullah Al Mamun, Md Nazmul Alam, Md Wasim Akram, Md Arif Hossain, Md Sayed Molla, Tarikul Islam Mintu, Sabbir Hossain, Mofiz, Md Arman Ali, Md Nazrul Islam, Md Aminur Islam, Kazi Rezaul Karim, Main Uddin, Ripon Hossain and Arif Hossain Patwari; Prothom Alo spoke to relatives of seven more of the 30 and said nearly all the families are low-income.
why_new: The names of the dead as the families give them, for the record; no official list exists.

claim: The six of the 30 still being made to fight in October 2026 are Roni Sheikh and Sourav Molla of Gopalganj, Al Amin Islam of Lalmonirhat, Kamal Hossain and Helal Sheikh of Madaripur and Abu Hanif of Kishoreganj, some of whom keep in contact with their families, Prothom Alo reported.
why_new: Names and home districts of the six still in the Russian army.

claim: According to BMET data reported by Prothom Alo on 27 October 2026, 4 thousand 727 Bangladeshis went to the Russian Federation in 2025, placing Russia 13th among destinations for Bangladeshi workers that year.
why_new: A 2025 BMET outflow figure for Russia; check against the Russia section's existing numbers.

claim: A draft report by the UN's Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine, published on the website of the UN human rights office (OHCHR) on 26 October 2026, examined information on the recruitment of nationals of 48 countries into Russia's forces and found evidence of deception or coercion for 29, Bangladesh among them; the report gives no separate figures on Bangladeshi recruits, their names or what happened to them.
why_new: Identifies the report, its date and its limits; the guide cites only '29 countries'.

claim: The UN commission obtained copies of business visas of recruited Bangladeshis that mention an invitation from a Russian civilian company, Prothom Alo reported on 28 October 2026.
why_new: The visa type actually used for Bangladeshis: a business visa on a civilian company's invitation, not a work visa.

claim: The UN commission's report describes a group of 30 who were given a letter of assurance saying they would not be sent to the Russia-Ukraine battlefield; by the time the report was written 17 of the group had been killed on the front line, 5 were missing and 1 had returned wounded; the report does not name the group's country.
why_new: A written 'you will not be sent to the war' guarantee was given and was worthless.

claim: According to the UN commission, men abroad got Russian job offers through social media adverts or through recruiting agents and firms, for work as security guards, drivers, mechanics, electricians, construction workers, welders, repair workers, transport workers and technicians, and in some cases in IT, medicine, sport or agriculture; some recruiters said the work was under the military but civilian.
why_new: The full range of jobs used as bait, and the 'under the military but civilian' line.

claim: The UN commission says the job offers spoke of high pay, Russian citizenship, comfortable housing, a pension after leaving the job and other benefits, and that some recruits were shown photos or a catalogue of the housing.
why_new: What is promised and the props used (housing photos, a catalogue).

claim: The UN commission found that after accepting, many recruits were pressed to travel to Russia within a few days; agents arranged the visa, air ticket, housing and the rest of the journey; some paid in advance and others were told the money would be deducted from their pay later; and visa types varied by country and region between business visas, short-term tourist visas and no visa at all.
why_new: Pressure to leave within days, the 'pay later from salary' variant and the visa types.

claim: Testimony and documents obtained by the UN commission name Bahrain, Brazil, Ethiopia, France, Kenya, Mexico, Morocco, Oman, Panama, Spain, Turkey and the United Arab Emirates as transit countries; in some cases agents travelled with the recruits or met them in the transit country, and some recruits were told to go by road to a neighbouring country and fly from there so as not to be caught at the airport.
why_new: Transit countries and the instruction to leave from a neighbouring country to avoid airport checks.

claim: The UN commission says the recruiting agents in the various countries were local, regional or Russian nationals who operated as travel or tourism businesses; some firms held local licences, some presented themselves as legal or government-approved, and in many cases visas issued by the Russian embassy were handed over through the agents.
why_new: Who the recruiters are (travel and tourism firms, some licensed) and that the embassy visa itself comes through them.

claim: According to the UN commission, many recruits had no freedom of movement after reaching the airport in Russia: they were kept in temporary accommodation, handed to the Russian armed forces, and within hours or days of arriving made to sign a one-year military service contract with Russia's Defence Ministry.
why_new: The contract is with the Russian Defence Ministry, for one year, and is signed within hours or days.

claim: The UN commission found the contracts were written in Russian, most recruits did not know Russian and so could not understand the terms, and they could not use translation because their phones were not in their hands.
why_new: Why the men could not translate the contract: the phones had already been taken.

claim: The UN commission's report says recruits who refused to sign the contract were pressured, threatened or tortured; one recruit said four people were shot dead in front of him and he was told he would be next if he did not sign, after which he signed.
why_new: What refusal to sign leads to.

claim: According to the UN commission, initial military training lasted from 20 minutes to a few days, in some cases up to a month; the recruits were then sent to battlefields in Ukraine, where they were made to dig trenches, guard areas, deliver food and water and collect bodies, their main tasks being to carry out assaults and advance; they also reported days without food and water, beatings, detention and death threats.
why_new: Training length (as little as 20 minutes) and the tasks, from a UN source.

claim: The UN commission found that recruits were taken to open bank accounts, but many were not paid and some got little; money was withdrawn from some accounts without permission, some salaries were withheld or accounts closed, and in some cases recruiting agents or military personnel took the bank cards; many recruits lost contact with their families after going to the war.
why_new: How the pay disappears: the bank card is taken by the agent or military staff.

claim: The UN commission concluded that the Russian authorities committed human trafficking together with recruiting agents; that because trafficked people became members of the Russian armed forces on signing the contract they cannot be called mercenaries; and that if they surrender or are captured they are entitled to prisoner-of-war protection until the war ends.
why_new: The men's legal status under international law (not mercenaries; prisoner-of-war protection on capture or surrender).

claim: The UN commission recommended that Russia stop recruiting foreign nationals through deception or coercion, discharge trafficked people who are in its forces and assist them, and investigate and prosecute those involved in the recruitment; according to international media citing its UN mission, Russia does not recognise the commission's mandate and says the report is based on false information.
why_new: The recommendation to discharge trafficked recruits, and Russia's rejection of the report.

claim: The UN commission's findings on recruitment rest on 245 testimonies from recruits detained by Ukrainian authorities or who got home, family members, lawyers, local authorities, researchers and journalists, plus invitation letters, itineraries, air tickets, visas, Russian entry documents, hotel bookings, military contracts and Russian Defence Ministry documents; the victims were all men aged 18 to 60, mostly from financially weak and marginal groups.
why_new: How the UN figure was established and who the victims are.

claim: Expatriates' Welfare Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury told Prothom Alo in October 2026 that extra caution is being taken over sending workers to Russia, that instructions have been given to check appointment letters much more thoroughly, and that action has begun against the recruiting agencies involved.
why_new: The government's response to the UN report.

claim: Selim Reza, coordinator of North South University's Centre for Migration Studies, told Prothom Alo in October 2026 that the government went on giving clearance for Russia even after learning that people were being taken to the war by force, and that the demand in Russia's labour market had not been properly assessed.
why_new: An academic's statement that clearances continued after the forced recruitment was known.

claim: The UN commission's report describes a professional athlete who was told Russia was taking foreign players and that he could sign a contract after arriving if he liked the work, and who was handed to the military on arrival; another recruit said he was a cook and did not want to be a soldier but ended up on the front line.
why_new: Two individual cases from the UN report showing the 'sign after you see the job' pitch and that a cook's job ends at the front.

claim: The UN commission sent 69 letters to various countries about the recruitment and received 6 replies, and its report says Russia did not answer 41 written requests.
why_new: How little governments, and Russia, cooperated with the UN inquiry.

claim: UN experts, in a statement published on the OHCHR website on 19 April 2024, said Bangladeshi workers were promised jobs before going to Malaysia but did not get the promised work after entering, and that many were forced to stay on after their visas expired, putting them at risk of arrest, detention, ill-treatment and deportation.
